Fever and warm, flushed skin are not expected; low body temperature and cold intolerance are more typical. Recognizing these findings helps the nurse see that an eating disorder is a medical as well as a psychological problem.
questions.takeaway: Lanugo, bradycardia, and orthostatic changes are physical cues of severe restriction that need medical evaluation.
questions.hintContent: Think about how the body conserves energy when intake is severely limited.
questions.hintStrategy: For SATA findings items, evaluate each option against the underlying mechanism rather than guessing by pattern.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old client tells the nurse, “I make myself throw up after I eat too much.” Which questions should the nurse ask during the initial assessment? Select all that apply.
options: “How often does this happen in a typical week?”
“Have you had dizziness, fainting, or a racing heartbeat?”
“Do you use laxatives, diuretics, or other pills to lose weight?”
“Why can’t you simply stop once you know it is harmful?”
“Have you thought about just eating smaller portions instead?”
optionRationales: Correct. Frequency helps determine severity and medical risk.
Correct. These symptoms may indicate dehydration, electrolyte imbalance, or dysrhythmia.
Correct. Other compensatory methods add to fluid and electrolyte risk.
Incorrect. A “why” question is judgmental and may shame the client into silence.
Incorrect. Offering advice is premature and minimizes the problem.
questions.rationale: An initial assessment of purging focuses on frequency, physical symptoms, and all compensatory methods, because these determine medical risk. Dizziness, fainting, and palpitations can signal dehydration, hypokalemia, or dysrhythmias that need prompt evaluation. Asking “why” sounds direct but implies the problem is a matter of willpower and can end the conversation. Suggesting smaller portions offers premature advice that minimizes a serious problem.
questions.takeaway: Assess frequency, physical symptoms, and all compensatory behaviors without judgment.
questions.hintContent: Select questions that help determine how dangerous the behavior is right now.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate “why” questions and advice in assessment items; keep questions that gather data.

questions.stem: The nurse teaches the parents of an 11-year-old who has started making negative comments about her body. Which statements by the parents indicate understanding of how to support a healthy body image? Select all that apply.
options: “We will praise her effort and skills instead of her weight.”
“We will avoid joking about anyone’s body size at home.”
“We will weigh her weekly in front of the family to keep her on track.”
“We will look for physical activities she actually enjoys.”
“We will start her on a diet now so that she does not gain weight later.”
optionRationales: Correct. Praising effort and skills reduces the link between body size and worth.
Correct. Discouraging appearance-based teasing reduces shame.
Incorrect. Public weigh-ins increase shame and focus on body size.
Correct. Enjoyable activity supports participation without making weight the focus.
Incorrect. Dieting reinforces body-size concerns and is not a body-image strategy.
questions.rationale: Supportive environments discourage appearance-based teasing, avoid public weigh-ins, and encourage enjoyable activity. Praising effort, skills, and personal strengths rather than body size helps separate worth from appearance. Weekly family weigh-ins are tempting to parents who want accountability, but they increase shame and focus on weight. Starting a diet reinforces the very concerns the parents are trying to reduce.
questions.takeaway: Support body image by praising strengths, avoiding weight talk and public weigh-ins, and encouraging enjoyable activity.
questions.hintContent: Ask whether each statement focuses attention on body size or on the child’s strengths.
questions.hintStrategy: For teaching evaluation items, select statements that reduce shame and eliminate those that increase focus on weight.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client has expressive aphasia after a stroke. Which observations should the nurse recognize as cues suggesting low self-esteem that warrant further exploration? Select all that apply.
options: Refuses group therapy, writing “I am useless” on his board
Writes that he is “just a burden on everyone” now
Asks for help cutting the meat on his lunch tray
Practices his speech exercises with the therapist daily
Has stopped shaving, which his wife says he did every day for 40 years
optionRationales: Correct. Self-devaluing words and withdrawal from activities suggest low self-esteem.
Correct. Seeing himself as a burden reflects low self-worth and also warrants safety assessment.
Incorrect. Asking for appropriate help is adaptive and reflects realistic self-assessment.
Incorrect. Engaging in rehabilitation suggests motivation and hope.
Correct. Abandoning a long-standing self-care routine can signal low self-worth and needs exploration.
questions.rationale: Low self-esteem may appear as self-devaluing statements, withdrawal from activities, and neglect of long-valued routines. Each of these cues warrants exploration, and statements about being a burden also call for a safety assessment. Asking for help with a task he cannot do is adaptive rather than a sign of low self-worth. Daily participation in speech therapy suggests motivation and hope.
questions.takeaway: Self-devaluing words, withdrawal, and abandoned routines are cues of low self-esteem; asking for appropriate help is not.
questions.hintContent: Separate behaviors that show giving up from those that show realistic adaptation.
questions.hintStrategy: In cue-recognition SATA items, select only findings that point toward the named problem.

questions.stem: A client recovering from facial surgery for skin cancer says, “I do not want my partner to see me until the swelling is gone.” Which possibilities should the nurse keep in mind while exploring this statement? Select all that apply.
options: Fear of the partner’s reaction to the change in appearance
Concern for her safety within the relationship
A personal need for privacy during early recovery
Evidence that the client has a personality disorder
Proof that the relationship is ending
A sign that she wants no emotional support
optionRationales: Correct. Anticipated rejection is a common body-image concern after visible surgery.
Correct. The statement may reflect relationship safety, which the nurse must not overlook.
Correct. Wanting privacy may be a reasonable personal preference rather than a problem.
Incorrect. One statement about a partner provides no basis for a personality diagnosis.
Incorrect. The statement does not establish anything about the relationship’s future.
Incorrect. Avoiding the partner does not mean she declines all support; that must be asked.
questions.rationale: A statement like this can reflect body-image distress, fear of rejection, relationship safety, or a simple need for privacy. The nurse should keep several explanations in mind and explore with open-ended questions rather than assume one cause. Asking privately about safety in the relationship is part of a complete assessment. Concluding that the relationship is ending, that she has a personality disorder, or that she wants no support goes far beyond the data.
questions.takeaway: One statement can have several meanings; explore body image, fear, safety, and privacy before assuming a cause.
questions.hintContent: List every reason a person might not want a partner to see them right now.
questions.hintStrategy: In hypothesis SATA items, select possibilities the data support and eliminate conclusions stated as certainty.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old client with anorexia nervosa is on day 3 of a nutrition-restoration plan. Review the exhibit. Which findings should the nurse report to the provider as possible signs of refeeding syndrome? Select all that apply.
options: Phosphorus 1.7 mg/dL
Potassium 3.1 mEq/L
Magnesium 1.2 mEq/L
Sodium 138 mEq/L
Glucose 88 mg/dL
Weight gain of 0.4 kg since admission
optionRationales: Correct. Low phosphorus is the hallmark electrolyte change of refeeding syndrome.
Correct. Potassium shifts into cells during refeeding and can cause dysrhythmias.
Correct. Low magnesium is part of the refeeding pattern and increases dysrhythmia risk.
Incorrect. This sodium level is within the reference range.
Incorrect. This glucose level is within the reference range.
Incorrect. Gradual weight gain is an expected goal of nutrition restoration.
questions.rationale: When nutrition is restarted after severe restriction, insulin release drives phosphate, potassium, and magnesium into cells, lowering serum levels. Phosphorus 1.7 mg/dL, potassium 3.1 mEq/L, and magnesium 1.2 mEq/L are all below their reference ranges and can lead to weakness, respiratory compromise, and dysrhythmias. Sodium and glucose are normal. Gradual weight gain is the intended outcome of treatment, not a complication.
questions.takeaway: Refeeding syndrome lowers phosphate, potassium, and magnesium; report these early in nutrition restoration.
questions.hintContent: Compare each value with its reference range and recall which electrolytes shift into cells when feeding resumes.
questions.hintStrategy: In lab SATA items, check each value against its range and the condition named in the stem.

questions.stem: A 23-year-old client has a positive SCOFF screen, lanugo, and a 9-kg weight loss over 3 months. Which team members should the nurse anticipate involving in the client’s care? Select all that apply.
options: A mental-health professional for evaluation and therapy
A registered dietitian for nutrition assessment and planning
The primary provider to evaluate medical complications
A personal trainer to design a weight-maintenance exercise plan
The employer’s human resources office to arrange schedule changes
optionRationales: Correct. Comprehensive psychological evaluation and treatment are needed after a positive screen.
Correct. Nutrition restoration requires specialized planning, not a nurse-designed regimen.
Correct. Lanugo and weight loss suggest physical effects that need medical evaluation.
Incorrect. Exercise planning by a trainer is not part of eating-disorder treatment and may reinforce compensatory behavior.
Incorrect. Contacting an employer without consent violates privacy and is not part of the clinical team.
questions.rationale: A positive screen with physical findings calls for coordinated interprofessional care. The mental-health professional provides diagnosis and therapy, the dietitian plans nutrition restoration, and the provider evaluates medical complications such as electrolyte and cardiac effects. The nurse supports coping and monitors the plan but does not independently design an aggressive feeding regimen. A personal trainer may reinforce compensatory exercise, and contacting an employer without consent violates privacy.
questions.takeaway: Eating disorders require coordinated mental-health, nutrition, and medical care.
questions.hintContent: Think about which disciplines address the mind, the nutrition, and the body.
questions.hintStrategy: For team-member SATA items, choose disciplines with a clear clinical role and eliminate those that breach privacy.
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating a 45-year-old client’s adaptation 2 weeks after a below-the-knee amputation. Which behaviors suggest the client is beginning to integrate the change in body image? Select all that apply.
options: Looks at the residual limb during the dressing change
Asks when he can be fitted for a prosthesis
Keeps the limb covered with a blanket during all visits
Touches the residual limb while learning to wrap it
States, “I will never let my kids see me like this.”
optionRationales: Correct. Looking at the limb shows growing acceptance of the change.
Correct. Planning for a prosthesis shows engagement with life after the change.
Incorrect. Consistent concealment suggests ongoing avoidance rather than integration.
Correct. Touching and caring for the limb is a concrete sign of integration.
Incorrect. This statement shows continued distress and avoidance, not integration.
questions.rationale: Integration of a body-image change is shown through behavior: looking at, touching, and caring for the changed body part, and planning for future function. Looking at the limb, touching it during care, and asking about a prosthesis are concrete signs of progress. Constant concealment and refusing to let family see the change suggest ongoing distress that needs continued support. Recovery may be gradual, so the nurse does not demand immediate acceptance.
questions.takeaway: Integration of a body change appears as looking at, touching, caring for, and planning around the change.
questions.hintContent: Look for behaviors that move toward the changed body part rather than away from it.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation SATA items, choose observable behaviors that show progress toward the stated goal.

questions.stem: A nurse learns that a colleague has given her personal cell phone number to a client on the unit and has been texting the client every evening. The colleague says, “Please do not tell anyone. It is really helping her.” What is the nurse’s best action?
options: Report the situation to the nurse manager.
Agree to keep the situation confidential for now.
Text the client to explain the boundary.
Wait to see whether the texting stops.
optionRationales: Correct. Ongoing personal contact is a boundary violation, and reporting to the manager follows the chain of command.
Incorrect. Keeping the secret allows a boundary violation that can harm the client to continue.
Incorrect. Contacting the client personally repeats the violation and bypasses the proper process.
Incorrect. Waiting allows the boundary violation to continue.
questions.rationale: Ongoing personal contact with a client outside the professional role is a boundary violation, even when the nurse believes it helps. Boundaries protect the purpose and safety of the therapeutic relationship, and a request for secrecy is itself a warning sign. Because the colleague has asked for silence and the contact continues, the nurse follows the chain of command by reporting to the nurse manager. Keeping quiet or waiting is tempting to protect a coworker, but it allows potential harm to the client to continue.
questions.takeaway: Boundary violations that continue in secret are reported through the chain of command.
questions.hintContent: Consider whose interests the professional boundary protects.
questions.hintStrategy: When client welfare is at risk from a colleague’s conduct, choose the option that escalates through the chain of command.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A 30-year-old client admitted for depression and low self-esteem says to the nurse, “I will tell you something important, but only if you promise not to tell anyone else.” Which response should the nurse make?
options: “I cannot promise that, because safety concerns must be shared with the team.”
“You can trust me. Whatever you say will stay between the two of us.”
“It is fine if you would rather not share. We can talk about it later.”
“I will only tell your provider if I think it is something really serious or dangerous.”
optionRationales: Correct. This is honest about the limits of confidentiality while still inviting the client to talk.
Incorrect. A promise of secrecy may have to be broken, which would damage trust.
Incorrect. Postponing may close the door on an important disclosure.
Incorrect. This is still a misleading promise with a vague condition.
questions.rationale: Trust is built on honesty, so the nurse must not make a promise that may have to be broken. Explaining up front that information affecting safety is shared with the treatment team keeps the relationship honest and still invites the client to talk. Promising secrecy is tempting because it seems to build rapport, but it sets up a betrayal if the client discloses self-harm plans. Postponing the conversation may lose an important disclosure, and a vague condition about something “really serious” is still misleading.
questions.takeaway: Never promise secrecy; explain honestly that safety information is shared with the team.
questions.hintContent: Think about what happens to trust if the client reveals a plan to harm herself.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the honest response that keeps the conversation open over one that buys rapport with a false promise.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client who had facial surgery 2 days ago is found in the bathroom holding a disposable razor and crying, “I cannot live looking like this.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reassure the client that the swelling will improve in a few weeks.
Leave to notify the provider of the client’s statement right away.
Stay with the client and call for help while asking for the razor.
Ask the client to describe what she sees when she looks in the mirror.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Reassurance does not address the immediate danger.
Incorrect. Leaving the client alone with a means of self-harm could be fatal.
Correct. Staying, summoning help, and removing the means address immediate risk of self-harm.
Incorrect. Body-image exploration is appropriate only after immediate safety is secured.
questions.rationale: A client expressing a wish not to live while holding a potential means of self-harm is at immediate risk. The nurse stays with the client, summons help, and calmly asks for the razor so the means can be removed. Notifying the provider is tempting because it is necessary, but leaving the client alone even briefly could be fatal. Exploring body-image feelings and offering reassurance are appropriate only after immediate safety is secured.
questions.takeaway: With immediate self-harm risk, stay with the client, get help, and remove the means before anything else.
questions.hintContent: Ask what could happen if the nurse leaves the room.
questions.hintStrategy: Never leave a client at imminent risk alone; call for help from the bedside.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 22-year-old client began sertraline for major depression and low self-worth 10 days ago. Review the exhibit. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Document that the medication is improving the client’s mood.
Ask the client directly whether he is thinking about suicide.
Encourage the client to attend the afternoon self-esteem group.
Teach the client that sertraline’s full benefit takes 4 to 6 weeks.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Increased energy in this context signals danger rather than recovery.
Correct. Sudden calm, giving away a valued possession, and “made my plans” early in antidepressant therapy are suicide warning signs.
Incorrect. Group participation is appropriate later but does not address possible imminent risk.
Incorrect. Teaching about onset is accurate but does not address the warning signs present now.
questions.rationale: Early in antidepressant therapy, energy can improve before mood does, which can give a depressed client the energy to act on suicidal thoughts; antidepressants carry a boxed warning about suicidality in children and young adults. Sudden calm, giving away a valued possession, and saying he has “made his plans” are classic warning signs. The nurse asks directly about suicidal thoughts and plans and follows the safety protocol. Documenting improvement is tempting because the client is up and showered, but these changes in context signal danger.
questions.takeaway: Sudden calm, giving away possessions, and new energy early in antidepressant therapy call for a direct suicide assessment.
questions.hintContent: Compare the two notes and ask what could explain the sudden change.
questions.hintStrategy: When improvement appears suddenly alongside warning signs, assume risk until a direct assessment rules it out.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies

rows: In bed most of the day. Flat affect. States, “I am worthless. Nothing I do matters.”
Up early, showered, and dressed. Gave his guitar to his roommate. States, “I feel calm now that I have made my plans.”

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke agreed yesterday to brush his own teeth at the sink with standby assistance. Today he stays in bed and says, “Just do it for me.” What should the nurse do first?
options: Document that the client is noncompliant with the self-care plan.
Remind him that he agreed to this goal and should follow through.
Brush his teeth for him and remove the goal from the care plan.
Ask what is different today, including pain, fatigue, or mood.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Labeling noncompliance treats the result as a moral failure rather than information.
Incorrect. This treats the setback as defiance and may damage trust and self-esteem.
Incorrect. Abandoning the goal before knowing the barrier gives up a meaningful step.
Correct. Assessing why a goal was not met identifies barriers before the plan is changed.
questions.rationale: When a client does not meet an agreed goal, the nurse first assesses why; pain, fatigue, mood, understanding, or readiness may all interfere. The result is information, not a moral failure. Holding him to his agreement or documenting noncompliance treats the setback as defiance and can damage self-esteem and trust. Taking over and removing the goal is tempting because it avoids conflict, but it abandons a meaningful step before the nurse knows what got in the way.
questions.takeaway: When a goal is not met, assess the barrier before revising the plan or judging the client.
questions.hintContent: Consider what might have changed since yesterday.
questions.hintStrategy: Assess before acting: choose the option that gathers information about the setback.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client on a medical unit who became physically aggressive toward staff has been calmed with verbal de-escalation and is now resting. As charge nurse, what should the nurse do first?
options: Update the care plan with the client’s known triggers.
Hold a team debriefing to review what went well.
Check the client and involved staff for any injuries.
Document the incident in the client’s health record.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Updating the plan supports consistency but is not the first priority.
Incorrect. Debriefing is important but follows assessment for injuries.
Correct. After an aggressive episode, physical safety of everyone involved comes first.
Incorrect. Documentation is required but follows care of anyone who may be injured.
questions.rationale: After an aggressive episode ends, the first priority is the physical safety of everyone involved, so the client and staff are checked for injuries that need treatment. Debriefing, updating the plan with triggers, and documenting observable behavior and response are all important and should follow promptly. Debriefing is tempting because it supports staff and team consistency, but it cannot come before addressing possible harm. Safety, then communication and documentation, is the usual order.
questions.takeaway: After an aggressive incident, check everyone for injury first; debrief, plan, and document afterward.
questions.hintContent: Think about which need could worsen if it waits.
questions.hintStrategy: When all options are correct actions, order them: physical safety, then communication, then documentation.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control

questions.stem: The mother of a 27-year-old client admitted for an eating disorder calls the unit and asks how her daughter is doing and whether she has been eating. The client has not authorized anyone to receive information. What should the nurse do first?
options: Transfer the call to the client’s room so that the two can talk.
Share general progress only, because the mother is the client’s next of kin.
Tell the mother that her daughter is eating well and is doing fine.
Explain that information cannot be shared without the client’s permission.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Transferring the call confirms her presence and removes the client’s choice.
Incorrect. Next-of-kin status does not authorize disclosure without the client’s agreement.
Incorrect. Sharing any details without permission violates privacy.
Correct. An adult client controls who receives her health information.
questions.rationale: An adult client controls who receives her health information, and including family requires her agreement under privacy rules. The nurse explains that information cannot be shared without permission and can later ask the client whether she wants her mother involved. Sharing “general” progress is tempting because the mother is family and concerned, but next-of-kin status does not authorize disclosure. Transferring the call without asking also reveals that the client is on the unit and removes her choice.
questions.takeaway: Include family only with the adult client’s agreement; concern or kinship does not authorize disclosure.
questions.hintContent: Identify who decides what information is shared about an adult client.
questions.hintStrategy: In privacy items, choose the response that protects confidentiality while remaining courteous to the caller.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care

questions.stem: A client who had a radical neck dissection with tracheostomy 4 days ago gestures for a mirror for the first time. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Ask what the client expects to see and describe the changes before giving the mirror.
Hand the mirror over right away so the client feels in control of the situation.
Tell the client to wait until the swelling has gone down before looking at the incision.
Offer the mirror and then leave the room to give the client privacy for a while.
optionRationales: Correct. Preparing the client for what they will see reduces shock and supports adaptation.
Incorrect. Immediate access without preparation can be overwhelming at a vulnerable moment.
Incorrect. This overrides the client’s signal of readiness to see the change.
Incorrect. Leaving removes support when the client may need it most.
questions.rationale: Seeing a major change in appearance for the first time can be overwhelming, so the nurse prepares the client by exploring expectations and describing what they will see, then stays to offer support. The client’s readiness to look should be respected rather than delayed. Handing the mirror over immediately is tempting because it seems to honor autonomy, but it skips preparation. Leaving the client alone removes support at a vulnerable moment.
questions.takeaway: When a client is ready to see a body change, prepare them first and stay to support them.
questions.hintContent: Consider what the client needs before, during, and after the first look.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that respects readiness while providing preparation and presence.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 41-year-old firefighter with healing burns to both hands is frustrated about needing help with every meal. Which goal is the most appropriate initial goal to support his self-efficacy?
options: Client will verbalize acceptance of his altered hands before discharge.
Client will feed himself breakfast with adaptive utensils within 1 week.
Client will return to full duty as a firefighter within one month.
Client will state that the appearance of his hands no longer matters to him.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Demanding emotional acceptance sets a goal he may not be ready to meet.
Correct. This goal is specific, realistic, measurable, and directly addresses his frustration.
Incorrect. This is unrealistic for healing burns and sets him up for failure.
Incorrect. Requiring this statement dismisses a real loss and is not a measurable functional goal.
questions.rationale: Self-efficacy grows through successful experiences with achievable, meaningful tasks. Self-feeding with adaptive utensils is specific, measurable, realistic, and directly addresses his stated frustration. Demanding acceptance or a statement that appearance does not matter sets an emotional goal the client may not be ready for. A return to full duty within a month is tempting because it matches his valued role, but it is unrealistic for healing burns and would undermine confidence.
questions.takeaway: Build self-efficacy with a small, specific, realistic goal tied to what matters most to the client now.
questions.hintContent: Look for the goal the client could actually achieve soon that addresses his stated frustration.
questions.hintStrategy: For goal-selection items, choose the option that is specific, measurable, realistic, and client-centered.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: An assistive personnel reports that while helping a client with a new colostomy bathe, the client cried and said, “Everyone would be better off without me.” The assistive personnel adds, “I told her not to talk like that.” What should the RN do first?
options: Teach the assistive personnel a better way to respond.
Go to the client now to assess for thoughts of suicide.
Notify the provider about the client’s statement.
Arrange for an ostomy nurse to visit the client today.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Coaching is important, but it can wait until the client is safe.
Correct. The statement may indicate suicidal thinking, and assessment is the RN’s responsibility and cannot be delegated.
Incorrect. The provider should be notified after the RN assesses the client’s risk.
Incorrect. An ostomy referral supports body image but does not address immediate risk.
questions.rationale: A statement that others would be better off without her may indicate suicidal thinking and requires immediate assessment by the RN; assessment cannot be delegated. The RN goes to the client first to assess risk directly and keep her safe. Coaching the assistive personnel is tempting because the response was nontherapeutic, but it can wait until the client is safe. Notifying the provider follows the RN’s assessment, and an ostomy referral addresses body image but not the immediate risk.
questions.takeaway: A reported statement suggesting suicide requires the RN’s immediate, direct assessment of the client.
questions.hintContent: Decide which concern in the report could put the client in danger.
questions.hintStrategy: Assessment belongs to the RN; when a report suggests risk, see the client before addressing staff or referrals.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: The charge nurse reviews the day assignments shown in the exhibit. Which assignment should be changed?
options: Assistive personnel teaching pouch care to the client with a new ileostomy
RN completing the admission assessment for the client after a suicide attempt
LPN reinforcing meal-plan teaching for the client with anorexia nervosa
Assistive personnel helping the stable client after mastectomy to shower
optionRationales: Correct. Initial teaching requires assessment and evaluation of learning and cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.
Incorrect. Admission and safety assessment of a high-risk client is appropriately assigned to the RN.
Incorrect. Reinforcing established teaching for a stable client is within LPN scope.
Incorrect. Assisting a stable client with hygiene while preserving privacy is appropriate to delegate.
questions.rationale: Initial teaching includes assessing learning needs and evaluating understanding, so it belongs to the RN and cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Teaching ostomy care to a client who may also be adjusting to a body-image change requires nursing judgment. Admission and safety assessment of a client after a suicide attempt is appropriately assigned to the RN. The LPN may reinforce teaching already provided, and assistive personnel may help a stable client shower while preserving privacy.
questions.takeaway: Assessment, initial teaching, and evaluation stay with the RN; hygiene for stable clients may be delegated.
questions.hintContent: Identify which task requires teaching and evaluation rather than routine care.
questions.hintStrategy: In assignment exhibits, check each task against the scope of the staff member assigned.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: On the day of discharge, a client who has worked with the nurse on coping with a new disability says, “You are the only person who really gets me. Can I have your phone number so we can keep talking?” Which response is best?
options: “You should not feel that way. Many people at home understand you, too.”
“Sure, but please call me only if something urgent comes up after you go home.”
“I am not allowed to, but you can find me on social media if you want to.”
“I cannot share my number, but let’s list people and services you can call.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Telling the client how not to feel dismisses the emotion.
Incorrect. Limiting calls to urgent matters still creates a personal relationship outside the professional role.
Incorrect. Social media contact is the same boundary violation in another form.
Correct. This states the boundary kindly and redirects the client to ongoing support.
questions.rationale: A therapeutic relationship is professional and time-limited, and personal contact after discharge crosses that boundary even when the request is sincere. The nurse kindly states the limit and redirects the client to supports such as a counselor, support group, or crisis line. Agreeing to urgent-only calls is tempting because it feels compassionate, but it still creates a personal relationship. Suggesting social media is the same violation, and telling the client not to feel that way dismisses the feeling.
questions.takeaway: State the professional boundary kindly and redirect the client to sustainable supports.
questions.hintContent: Consider whether the therapeutic relationship continues after discharge.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that maintains the boundary and still meets the client’s underlying need.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client with borderline personality disorder uses the call light every few minutes to ask the nurse for small favors and becomes upset when the nurse cannot come immediately. Which intervention is most appropriate?
options: Ignore the call light until the client learns to wait patiently.
Answer every call immediately so that the client does not feel abandoned.
Schedule brief check-ins at set times that all staff follow consistently.
Assign a different nurse each shift so that no one becomes overwhelmed.
optionRationales: Incorrect. Ignoring calls is unsafe and punitive.
Incorrect. This reinforces the pattern and is not sustainable.
Correct. Predictable structure applied by all staff reduces anxiety and repeated requests while maintaining the relationship.
Incorrect. Rotating staff increases inconsistency, which can worsen distress.
questions.rationale: Clear, predictable structure applied consistently by all staff reduces anxiety and repeated demands while maintaining the relationship. Scheduled check-ins tell the client when the nurse will return, and keeping them reliably builds trust, while urgent calls are still answered. Answering every call immediately is tempting because it avoids upset, but it reinforces the pattern and cannot be sustained. Ignoring the call light is unsafe, and rotating nurses increases inconsistency.
questions.takeaway: Consistent, scheduled contact that every staff member follows is a therapeutic limit, not a punishment.
questions.hintContent: Think about what reduces the client’s need to keep calling.
questions.hintStrategy: Prefer the option that is consistent, predictable, and team-based over extremes of giving in or withdrawing.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A college student receiving cognitive behavioral therapy for low self-esteem tells the nurse, “I failed one exam, so I am a complete failure at everything.” Which response best reinforces the treatment approach?
options: “Let’s focus on deep breathing to help you calm down now.”
“Do not be so hard on yourself; one exam is no big deal.”
“What evidence do you have that you fail at everything?”
“Tell me about your childhood and how your parents judged you.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Breathing is a useful coping tool but does not address the distorted thought.
Incorrect. Reassurance dismisses the feeling and does not teach a skill.
Correct. Examining evidence for an all-or-nothing thought reinforces a core CBT skill.
Incorrect. Exploring childhood belongs to other approaches and does not reinforce CBT.
questions.rationale: CBT examines the links among thoughts, feelings, and behavior and helps clients test distorted thoughts against evidence. Asking for evidence invites the student to examine the all-or-nothing belief rather than accept it. Reassurance is tempting because it sounds supportive, but it dismisses the feeling and does not teach a skill. Breathing addresses arousal rather than the thought, and exploring childhood does not reinforce this treatment approach.
questions.takeaway: Reinforce CBT by helping the client test a distorted thought against evidence.
questions.hintContent: Recall what CBT focuses on: thoughts, feelings, and behavior.
questions.hintStrategy: When the stem names a therapy, choose the response that uses that therapy’s specific technique.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 13-year-old hospitalized for an eating disorder becomes silent whenever the nurse asks about feelings but spends free time drawing in a sketchbook. Which nursing intervention best fits the teen’s current way of expressing emotions?
options: Invite the teen to use drawing or journaling to express feelings.
Insist that the teen answer questions about feelings at each visit.
Remove art supplies until the teen participates in talk therapy.
Ask the parents to explain the teen’s feelings to the care team.
optionRationales: Correct. Expressive approaches build on an existing strength and give another route for communication.
Incorrect. Pressure to talk may deepen withdrawal and harm trust.
Incorrect. Removing a valued activity is punitive and not therapeutic.
Incorrect. Parents speaking for the teen bypasses the adolescent’s own voice.
questions.rationale: Expressive approaches such as art and journaling give clients another route to communicate feelings when talking is difficult. Building on a teen’s existing interest is a strength-based way to support engagement and trust. Insisting on verbal answers is tempting because talk is the usual way to assess feelings, but pressure may deepen withdrawal. Removing supplies is punitive, and having parents speak for the teen bypasses the adolescent’s own voice.
questions.takeaway: When talking is hard, use the client’s preferred form of expression, such as art or journaling.
questions.hintContent: Notice what the teen already does comfortably.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the strength-based option that meets the client where they are.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: The wife of a client with a recent above-the-knee amputation insists on doing all of his care, including tasks he performed independently in rehabilitation. The client has become quiet and passive. Which action by the nurse is best?
options: Tell the client to insist that his wife stop helping him with everything.
Praise the wife’s devotion and let her continue providing all of his care.
Ask the wife to stop visiting until the client becomes more independent.
Teach the wife to encourage his independence and help only when needed.
optionRationales: Incorrect. This shifts the burden to the client without supporting either partner.
Incorrect. This reinforces dependence and may further lower his self-esteem.
Incorrect. Restricting visits damages a key support relationship.
Correct. Teaching the family to support what the client can do protects his confidence and independence.
questions.rationale: Families support self-concept when they encourage the client to do what he can and step in only when needed. The wife is likely trying to help, so the nurse teaches rather than blames, explaining how his participation protects his independence and confidence. Praising her devotion while letting her take over is tempting because her intentions are good, but it reinforces dependence. Restricting her visits or putting the burden on the client to confront her damages a key support relationship.
questions.takeaway: Teach families to support the client’s independence rather than take over care.
questions.hintContent: Consider what the client’s growing passivity suggests about the current arrangement.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the option that keeps the family involved while redirecting their help.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: During a conversation about his depression, a client asks the nurse, “Have you ever felt this hopeless?” Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
options: “Yes, after my divorce I felt hopeless for most of that year, too.”
“I have had hard times, but tell me what this hopelessness is like for you.”
“That is personal, and I do not share details of my private life with clients.”
“Everyone feels down sometimes, and it always gets better in time.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Detailed self-disclosure shifts the focus to the nurse.
Correct. A brief acknowledgment followed by a refocusing question keeps attention on the client.
Incorrect. A flat refusal can feel rejecting and close the conversation.
Incorrect. This is false reassurance that may make the client feel misunderstood.
questions.rationale: Therapeutic communication keeps the focus on the client. A brief acknowledgment followed by a refocusing question respects the client’s question while returning to his experience and allowing assessment of hopelessness, including safety. Sharing a personal story is tempting because it feels genuine, but it shifts attention to the nurse and can burden the client. A flat refusal feels rejecting, and promising that it always gets better is false reassurance.
questions.takeaway: Keep self-disclosure brief and return the focus to the client’s experience.
questions.hintContent: Ask whose feelings each response focuses on.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate responses that center the nurse, shut the client down, or offer false reassurance.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client on an inpatient behavioral health unit tells the nurse, “The evening nurse lets me keep my phone after 10 p.m. You are the mean one.” The team-agreed plan limits phone use after 10 p.m. Which response is best?
options: “I will make an exception tonight because the evening nurse already did.”
“The team plan is no phones after 10. I will check that we are all following it.”
“The evening nurse should not have done that, and I am going to report her for it.”
“If you keep comparing staff, you will lose your phone privileges entirely.”
optionRationales: Incorrect. Making exceptions reinforces inconsistency and confusion.
Correct. Restating the agreed plan calmly and following up with the team promotes consistency.
Incorrect. Criticizing a colleague to the client escalates conflict and splits the team.
Incorrect. Threatening punishment turns a limit into a penalty.
questions.rationale: Inconsistent rules increase confusion and conflict, and clients may highlight differences among staff. The nurse calmly restates the agreed plan and follows up with the team so everyone applies the same expectation. Making an exception is tempting because it avoids conflict, but it reinforces inconsistency. Criticizing the colleague to the client or threatening punishment escalates conflict and turns a limit into a punishment.
questions.takeaway: Respond to staff comparisons by restating the team plan calmly and restoring consistency behind the scenes.
questions.hintContent: Think about what the client needs to hear and what the team needs to do.
questions.hintStrategy: Choose the response that is consistent, nonpunitive, and does not criticize colleagues in front of the client.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department has been shouting at other clients in the waiting area while waiting for test results. Which statements by the nurse reflect therapeutic limit setting? Select all that apply.
options: “Shouting at others is not okay here. I will talk with you in the consult room.”
“You can wait in the quiet room or take a short walk with me.”
“I will check on your results only after you stop being difficult.”
“You are just trying to get attention by acting this way.”
“I want to understand your concern. Please lower your voice so we can talk.”
“If you yell one more time, security will remove you from the building.”
optionRationales: Correct. This names the behavior, sets the expectation, and offers a way forward.
Correct. Offering acceptable choices supports autonomy within the limit.
Incorrect. Withholding care as a reward is punitive, and “difficult” is a label.
Incorrect. Assigning a motive is judgmental and escalates conflict.
Correct. This acknowledges the concern while stating a clear expectation.
Incorrect. A threat escalates the situation rather than setting a respectful limit.
questions.rationale: Therapeutic limit setting states the observed behavior, the expectation, and acceptable choices in a calm tone. Acknowledging the underlying concern while asking for a lower voice keeps the focus on helping. Making care conditional on behavior is tempting as leverage, but essential care is never a reward. Assigning motives and issuing threats escalate conflict; if danger appears, staff follow the response plan rather than threaten.
questions.takeaway: Set limits by naming the behavior, stating the expectation, and offering choices without threats or withholding care.
questions.hintContent: Check each statement for a clear expectation, a respectful tone, and continued care.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that threaten, label, or bargain with essential care.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 35-year-old client admitted for depression says, “I am no good at anything.” The client denies thoughts of self-harm. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan of care to support self-esteem? Select all that apply.
options: Help the client identify one personal strength each day.
Set small, achievable goals with the client for each shift.
Give specific feedback when the client completes a task.
Tell the client to stop saying negative things about self.
Make daily decisions for the client to reduce stress.
optionRationales: Correct. Identifying strengths counters global negative self-evaluation.
Correct. Success with achievable goals builds self-efficacy.
Correct. Specific feedback helps the client recognize real accomplishments.
Incorrect. Commanding the client to stop dismisses feelings and teaches no skill.
Incorrect. Removing choices reduces autonomy and confidence.
questions.rationale: Self-esteem grows through recognizing strengths and experiencing success. Identifying a daily strength, setting small achievable goals, and giving specific feedback on real accomplishments all build self-efficacy. Telling the client to stop negative talk is tempting because it seems direct, but it dismisses feelings and teaches no skill. Making decisions for the client removes opportunities for autonomy and confidence.
questions.takeaway: Build self-esteem through strengths, achievable goals, and specific feedback, not commands or taking over.
questions.hintContent: Ask which interventions give the client a chance to experience success.
questions.hintStrategy: In planning SATA items, select interventions that increase the client’s participation and eliminate those that remove it.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A client admitted for low self-esteem after losing a job has a goal of increased self-worth. Which findings indicate progress toward the goal? Select all that apply.
options: Shares one personal strength during group therapy
Chooses which unit activity to attend each morning
Says “I feel better” but spends all day alone in bed
Agrees with every suggestion that staff members make
Asks the social worker for help updating a résumé
optionRationales: Correct. Identifying a strength publicly shows improved self-evaluation.
Correct. Making choices shows growing confidence and participation in decisions.
Incorrect. A positive statement without matching behavior is not enough evidence of progress.
Incorrect. Passive agreement may reflect low self-worth rather than improvement.
Correct. Planning to re-enter work shows hope and engagement with a valued role.
questions.rationale: Progress in self-concept is evaluated through behavior, participation, and function, not just a positive statement. Sharing a strength, making choices, and taking steps toward a valued role are concrete evidence of improvement. Saying “I feel better” is meaningful but is tempting to accept alone; when it does not match behavior, the nurse continues to assess. Agreeing with everything may reflect passivity rather than confidence.
questions.takeaway: Evaluate self-worth by concrete behavior and participation, not by a positive statement alone.
questions.hintContent: Look for findings where the client acts, chooses, or plans.
questions.hintStrategy: In evaluation items, prefer observable behavior over verbal reports that are contradicted by actions.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A preceptor reviews collaborative therapies with a new nurse on a behavioral health unit. Which statements by the new nurse indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
options: “CBT helps clients examine links among thoughts, feelings, and behavior.”
“DBT teaches skills such as mindfulness and distress tolerance.”
“A supportive talk with a client can be charted as a CBT session.”
“Antidepressants are a universal treatment for low self-worth.”
“Art or journaling can help clients who find it hard to talk.”
optionRationales: Correct. This accurately describes cognitive behavioral therapy.
Correct. Dialectical behavior therapy includes mindfulness, emotion regulation, and distress tolerance.
Incorrect. A brief supportive conversation should not be documented as a specialist psychotherapy protocol.
Incorrect. Medications target specific diagnosed symptoms; none universally treats low self-worth.
Correct. Expressive therapies offer another route for communicating feelings.
questions.rationale: CBT examines links among thoughts, feelings, and behavior, DBT teaches skills such as mindfulness and distress tolerance, and expressive therapies use art, music, or journaling. Nurses reinforce these skills within the treatment plan but do not document a supportive conversation as a full psychotherapy session. Medications target particular diagnosed symptoms and are not a substitute for a therapeutic plan. Believing medication fixes self-worth is tempting but leads to unrealistic teaching.
questions.takeaway: Know what each therapy does, reinforce within the plan, and never present medication as a universal fix.
questions.hintContent: Match each therapy name to its core method.
questions.hintStrategy: For “indicates understanding” SATA items, eliminate statements that overstate a treatment or the nurse’s role.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: An RN is caring for a stable client 3 days after a below-the-elbow amputation who avoids looking at the residual limb. Which tasks can the RN delegate to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.
options: Assist the client with bathing while maintaining privacy
Report any statements of hopelessness to the RN right away
Measure and record the client’s vital signs each shift
Teach the client how to wrap the residual limb
Evaluate how the client is adjusting to the change
optionRationales: Correct. Hygiene assistance for a stable client is within the scope of assistive personnel.
Correct. Reporting observations to the RN is an appropriate delegated responsibility.
Correct. Routine vital signs for a stable client may be delegated.
Incorrect. Teaching requires RN assessment and evaluation of learning.
Incorrect. Evaluation of adjustment requires nursing judgment and stays with the RN.
questions.rationale: Assistive personnel can perform routine care for stable clients, such as hygiene and vital signs, and report observations to the RN. Assessment, teaching, and evaluation require nursing judgment and stay with the RN. Asking assistive personnel to report hopeless statements is appropriate because they observe the client closely, but the RN performs the follow-up assessment. Teaching limb care is tempting to delegate because it is routine, but initial teaching requires evaluation of understanding.
questions.takeaway: Delegate routine care and reporting; keep assessment, teaching, and evaluation with the RN.
questions.hintContent: Sort each task into routine care or nursing judgment.
questions.hintStrategy: In delegation SATA items, eliminate any task with the words teach, assess, or evaluate.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: The daughter of a client with advanced Parkinson disease has been the sole caregiver for 2 years. Which findings suggest caregiver strain that the nurse should address? Select all that apply.
options: Reports sleeping only 3 to 4 hours most nights
Has canceled several of her own medical appointments
Says she snaps at her father and then feels guilty
Demonstrates a safe transfer technique during the visit
Says her sister helps with care every other weekend
optionRationales: Correct. Chronic sleep loss is a common sign of caregiver strain.
Correct. Neglecting her own health suggests caregiving demands exceed her resources.
Correct. Irritability and guilt are emotional signs of strain.
Incorrect. This shows competence, not strain.
Incorrect. Shared help is a resource rather than a sign of strain.
questions.rationale: Caregivers may be willing to help yet need skills, respite, or resources. Sleep deprivation, neglect of one’s own health, and irritability followed by guilt are signs that demands exceed resources and the nurse should assess further and offer support. Demonstrating safe technique is tempting to view as fine overall, but competence does not rule out strain. Help from a sister is a resource to build on.
questions.takeaway: Assess caregiver strain through sleep, self-care, and emotional cues, not just caregiving skill.
questions.hintContent: Focus on how the caregiving is affecting the daughter herself.
questions.hintStrategy: Select findings that describe a problem for the person named in the stem, not strengths or resources.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 44-year-old client receiving chemotherapy has started losing her hair and says, “I do not even look like myself anymore.” Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
options: Ask what the hair loss means to her and how she is coping.
Offer information about wigs, scarves, and resources when she is ready.
Encourage her to look in the mirror today so she can start accepting it.
Let her decide when and how to discuss the change with her family.
Remind her that hair grows back, so this is only a temporary problem.
optionRationales: Correct. Exploring meaning and coping individualizes support.
Correct. Practical adaptations offered at her pace support body image.
Incorrect. Forcing exposure before she is ready can increase distress.
Correct. Respecting her choices about disclosure supports autonomy and dignity.
Incorrect. Minimizing the loss dismisses its current meaning to her.
questions.rationale: Body-image support begins with exploring what the change means to the client and how she is coping. Practical adaptations such as wigs and scarves are offered at her pace, and she decides how and when to involve family. Reminding her that hair grows back is tempting because it is true, but it minimizes the present loss. Pushing her to look in the mirror before she is ready can increase distress.
questions.takeaway: Support body image by exploring meaning, offering adaptations at the client’s pace, and respecting her choices.
questions.hintContent: Consider which actions follow the client’s pace and which push or minimize.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that minimize the loss or force a step the client has not chosen.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43

questions.stem: A 32-year-old mother with a severe rheumatoid arthritis flare can no longer safely lift her 1-year-old and says, “What kind of mother cannot pick up her own baby?” Which nursing actions support her role performance? Select all that apply.
options: Explore which parenting tasks matter most to her.
Identify routines she can do seated, such as feeding or reading.
Refer her to occupational therapy for adaptive childcare equipment.
Teach her partner to take over all of the infant’s care for now.
Advise her to avoid caring for the baby until she is stronger.
optionRationales: Correct. Knowing what she values guides meaningful adaptation.
Correct. Adapted routines preserve her parenting role within current ability.
Correct. Collaboration with rehabilitation provides practical tools for role function.
Incorrect. Removing all parenting tasks deepens the role loss.
Incorrect. Complete withdrawal from care is unnecessary and harms her sense of role.
questions.rationale: Role loss is addressed by identifying tasks the person can still do and developing new ways to do them. Exploring what matters most, adapting routines to her current ability, and collaborating with occupational therapy preserve her role as a parent. Having her partner take over everything is tempting because it seems protective, but it deepens the loss. The goal is meaningful function and choice, not avoidance.
questions.takeaway: Preserve valued roles by adapting tasks to current ability rather than removing them.
questions.hintContent: Look for actions that keep her parenting in an adapted form.
questions.hintStrategy: Eliminate options that solve the task by taking the role away from the client.
questions.ref: Module 29 · Nursing Care & Collaborative Therapies · slides 24–30, 32–43
